concepts.decision: Prefer safe constructs/languages where suitable and enforce bounds/lifetime discipline; test unsafe interfaces and treat mitigations as layers.
concepts.definition: The property that software accesses memory only within valid bounds, lifetime, type, and ownership rules.
concepts.failureExample: Use-after-free or out-of-bounds access can corrupt data or transfer control to attacker-influenced code.
concepts.label: Memory Safety

concepts.decision: Validate/bound input and use safe APIs/structures/compiler/runtime protections; test edge and oversized input at every interface.
concepts.definition: Writing more data than a fixed buffer can hold, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially altering behavior or control flow.
concepts.failureExample: A 17th byte written into a 16-byte buffer can overwrite adjacent state.
concepts.label: Buffer Overflow

concepts.decision: Define the invariant, use synchronization/atomicity/idempotency as appropriate, and test forced interleavings and duplicate requests.
concepts.definition: A defect where correctness or security outcome depends on uncontrolled timing/interleaving of concurrent operations.
concepts.failureExample: Two withdrawals both see available funds before either update, violating the balance invariant.
concepts.label: Race Condition

concepts.decision: Choose coordination that preserves required integrity/authorization semantics and bound retries/timeouts.
concepts.definition: Execution of multiple tasks whose shared state, ordering, visibility, cancellation, and failures must be controlled.
concepts.failureExample: Parallel requests can bypass a single-use token rule if check and consume are not atomic.
concepts.label: Concurrency

concepts.decision: Apply quotas, timeouts, cancellation, backpressure, size/rate limits, and resilient failure handling based on service need.
concepts.definition: Loss of availability when requests, memory, CPU, files, connections, retries, or queues consume finite resources without adequate bounds.
concepts.failureExample: Unbounded file upload processing can exhaust workers and deny legitimate users service.
concepts.label: Resource Exhaustion

concepts.decision: Inventory/pin/review dependencies, assess update impact, test changes, and retain rollback/response ownership.
concepts.definition: Risk introduced when a library, runtime, platform, or policy dependency changes, is vulnerable, unsupported, malicious, or behaves unexpectedly.
concepts.failureExample: A library update can change authorization defaults even if application source did not change.
concepts.label: Dependency Risk

concepts.decision: Protect policy authorship/approval, validate changes, separate duties, stage/monitor rollout, log decisions, define safe failure, and retain rollback.
concepts.definition: Security capabilities whose policy, enforcement, configuration, or control plane is programmable and distributed across software-managed infrastructure/services.
concepts.failureExample: A compromised policy service can rapidly grant broad access across every connected workload.
concepts.label: Software Defined Security

misconceptions.claim: A managed runtime eliminates all denial-of-service risk.
misconceptions.correction: Allocation, parsing, concurrency, algorithmic complexity, queues, and dependencies can still exhaust resources.

outcome: Identify implementation-specific failure modes and select prevention, detection, and containment practices.

sections.body: Memory-unsafe operations can enable corruption or code execution; concurrency errors can violate invariants; unbounded resources can create denial of service. Prefer memory-safe constructs where suitable, bounds checks, ownership and lifetime discipline, synchronization, timeouts, quotas, cancellation, and targeted tests. Treat compiler and runtime protections as layers, not guarantees of correct authorization.
keyPoints: A race can bypass a check even when each individual operation appears valid.
Resource limits are security controls as well as reliability controls.
Language safety reduces classes of bugs but does not prevent logic or authorization flaws.
sections.title: Prevent unsafe state and resource behavior

sections.body: Software-defined security moves policy and enforcement into programmable services, agents, infrastructure, and configuration. Protect the control plane, validate policy changes, separate duties, test failure behavior, log decisions, pin dependencies, and provide safe rollback. Dependency updates and platform changes can silently alter enforcement.
keyPoints: Programmable control can scale both protection and misconfiguration.
Policy code requires review, testing, provenance, and runtime observability.
Containment and rollback matter when a shared enforcement service fails.
sections.title: Use code-driven enforcement with guardrails

sections.body: Memory, concurrency, resource, dependency, and programmable-policy failures can affect database/data-warehouse integrity and web/API behavior. Review data access invariants, authorization and audit paths, web request/output contexts, and failure behavior in the affected deployment; do not treat a language/runtime mitigation as proof that a higher-level access or data control is correct.
keyPoints: A memory-safe runtime does not prove transaction authorization or data isolation.
A policy engine needs protected control-plane identity, tested semantics, logging, and rollback.
sections.title: Connect memory and policy failures to database and web environments

options.feedback: Changed fact: One inventory unit remains. Two different customers submit distinct authorized reservation requests, each with a different request identifier; both workers read quantity 1 before either commits. Why this answer fails: “Reuse the original conclusion because the overall control family is unchanged” does not account for that changed condition. treatmentDispositions.rationale: The state model preserves the reviewed lost-update invariant: two authorized requests read the same remaining quantity, non-atomic writes oversell, and an atomic conditional transaction plus idempotency yields one commit and one safe retry. It uses a fixed quota-one authored interleaving rather than the reviewed manipulable balance-100/A60/B60 simulator and controls, so it is equivalent.

Implements the separate reviewed control-plane rollout as a four-state variant: signed reviewed policy artifact, 1% canary with predeclared deny/error/response-access thresholds, automatic expansion stop, immutable rollback, and revised retest. It is not counted as equivalent to the quota interleaving.

A mere lock-performance benchmark does not prove the invariant.
